items.streamTitle: Finland joined France’s nuclear deterrence initiative as Europe diversifies its security architecture
items.streamSummary: Finland joined France’s Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative on September 14, becoming the tenth participating country. The framework offers deeper consultation, joint exercises and the possibility of temporary deployments of nuclear-capable assets, while France’s president retains sole authority over nuclear use. Finnish officials say participation complements NATO rather than replacing it and does not mean Finland plans to host nuclear weapons in peacetime. The move is a concrete change in European deterrence architecture, but its actual effects on reassurance, Russian risk perceptions or deterrence behavior remain unmeasured.

items.streamTitle: European officials call a train strike coercive signaling—but the behavioral effect is still unknown
items.streamSummary: A Russian drone struck a passenger train near Ukraine’s border with Poland on September 13, shortly after a train carrying European diplomats had passed the area. France’s foreign minister said the strike was intended to intimidate and divide Europeans. The physical event and timing are observable, but the claimed intent remains an official interpretation, and there is not yet evidence that the strike actually reduced European cohesion or support for Ukraine. The episode is useful for separating what happened, what the sender may have intended, how audiences interpreted the act and whether behavior subsequently changed.

items.streamTitle: A reinforcement-trained neural network reproduced several human beat-synchronization patterns
items.streamSummary: A new peer-reviewed study trained a recurrent neural network to tap along with metronome cues using different reinforcement schemes. One reward structure produced several human-like timing effects at once: stronger correction of late than early taps, a tendency to tap slightly ahead of noisy cues, accurate continuation after the metronome stopped, and internal dynamics resembling previously observed synchronization patterns. The result is a useful example of mechanistic modeling because one compact learning rule generated multiple behavioral signatures. It does not establish that the human brain learns beat synchronization through the same mechanism, so model fit should not be confused with biological proof.

items.streamTitle: Connective political language reduced reactance—but did not increase likes or replies
items.streamSummary: A preregistered experiment with 2,032 participants tested political Facebook posts that expressed openness to other perspectives and humility about the speaker’s own position. Compared with standard disagreeable posts, this ‘connective language’ reduced psychological reactance, counter-arguing, and perceived threats to freedom, while increasing enjoyment and reading time. It did not significantly increase behavioral engagement such as liking or replying. The study therefore identifies a promising communication style for reducing defensive processing, but it also shows why lower reactance should not automatically be equated with greater persuasion or participation.

items.streamTitle: A military AI framework argues that analytic advantage depends on the whole data-to-decision system
items.streamSummary: A Joint Force Quarterly analysis argues that militaries are competing in the wrong AI race if they focus mainly on bigger models. Its ‘analytic diamond’ links strategy, computing infrastructure, data, model development, operational deployment, human-machine teaming and governance, emphasizing that failure anywhere in the chain can prevent useful capability from reaching the mission. The authors also argue that smaller specialized models may outperform frontier systems when they use better data and integrate more effectively. This is a practitioner framework supported by examples, not a controlled test demonstrating superior operational outcomes.

items.streamTitle: Repeating political opinions did not make them seem more true
items.streamSummary: Two preregistered experiments and a mini meta-analysis tested whether the classic illusory-truth effect extends to social and political opinion statements. Across 457 participants, repeated opinions were not judged meaningfully more true than novel ones, including when participants already agreed or disagreed with the statement. The finding narrows an often generalized influence principle: repetition can still affect familiarity, attention, memory, or salience, but it may not automatically increase perceived truth for evaluative political opinions. The result should be distinguished from the robust repetition effects documented for many factual claims.

items.streamTitle: Upvotes increased long-run knowledge contribution while added followers often did not
items.streamSummary: A randomized field experiment with 1,696 Zhihu users manipulated upvotes and follower counts for 53 days and tracked behavior over 303 days. Added upvotes increased answer volume, length and an LLM-based quality measure, with some effects lasting up to 100 days and larger gains among lower-reputation or less-active users. Added followers had little overall positive effect and sometimes reduced other forms of engagement. The interpretation that upvotes signal contribution-specific recognition while followers signal status is plausible but not directly proven, and synthetic followers plus LLM-scored quality create important measurement limitations.
items.attribution: Zhang & Luo — Production and Operations Management

items.streamTitle: Public political speech can look more polarized—and more left-leaning—than private opinion
items.streamSummary: Preregistered U.S. experiments on polarized race- and gender-related topics found that moderates were least willing to publish their views online, while willingness to speak increased toward ideological extremes and was highest among progressive respondents. Participants also perceived public opinion as more left-leaning than the private views researchers actually measured. The finding matters for social listening and audience analysis because visible discourse is produced by a self-selected subset of people. The pattern should not be assumed to generalize to every issue or platform, but it shows why public expression is not a neutral sample of private belief.
items.attribution: Morales & Samahita — Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization

items.streamTitle: Stronger misinformation moderation reduced platform use—and cut exposure to official information even more
items.streamSummary: A randomized social-media experiment in Pakistan compared standard after-the-fact moderation with stronger ex-ante controls on COVID-19 misinformation. The tougher moderation reduced daily platform use by about 19%. In this setting, official information was more trusted and circulated more widely than misinformation, so reduced usage caused exposure to official information to fall 29% more than exposure to misinformation. The result does not imply moderation is generally harmful; it shows that moderation can change who stays on a platform and what else they see. Evaluations therefore need to measure user exit and information substitution, not only content removal.
items.attribution: Hirshleifer et al. — Journal of Development Economics

items.streamTitle: Prediction models performed better when they anticipated how people would game them
items.streamSummary: An American Economic Review study develops ‘manipulation-robust’ prediction rules for settings where people can strategically change the features an algorithm observes. The authors explicitly model those incentives and stress-test the approach in a large field experiment in Kenya, where strategy-robust linear rules outperformed standard linear models such as LASSO. The broader lesson is important for any decision-support or targeting system: once a measure affects consequences, people may adapt to the measure. This is a prediction-and-incentives result, not evidence that every behavioral indicator will be manipulated or that the same solution fits every domain.
items.attribution: Björkegren, Blumenstock & Knight — American Economic Review

items.streamTitle: Stack Overflow retention fell in the generative-AI era, but social feedback kept its value
items.streamSummary: An analysis of 10,000 new Stack Overflow users found that upvotes, comments, and completing a profile were associated with greater retention, while downvotes and the period after ChatGPT’s introduction were associated with lower retention. The positive link between profile completion and staying weakened after generative AI arrived, while votes and comments remained relatively stable. One interpretation is that AI can substitute for some informational or autonomy-related benefits but not social interaction. Because the study is observational, it cannot prove ChatGPT caused the change.
items.attribution: Minhyung Kang — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.streamTitle: NATO allies say they disrupted a Russian undersea sabotage rehearsal near Svalbard
items.streamSummary: Reuters reports that British, Norwegian, and U.S. forces tracked and confronted Russian GUGI vessels near Svalbard after Western officials assessed that deep-sea submersibles were rehearsing how to disable critical undersea cables. No cable was damaged, and the vessels were reportedly prevented from completing the exercise. Norway says the operation was meant to show Russia that covert activity would be detected and met with consequences. The operational disruption is observable; whether the episode actually deters future Russian behavior has not been demonstrated.

items.streamTitle: Targeted phone tutoring worked across five countries and through government delivery
items.streamSummary: Five randomized trials in India, Kenya, Nepal, the Philippines, and Uganda found that weekly targeted phone tutoring plus SMS produced sizable learning gains during school disruptions, with a pooled numeracy effect of 0.321 standard deviations. SMS alone had a much smaller and less consistent effect. In Nepal and the Philippines, government teachers achieved large gains as well as NGO instructors, addressing a common scale-up problem. Effects varied by country and implementation improved over time, so the study supports the core model without implying identical performance everywhere.

items.streamTitle: Synthetic LLM surveys need an error framework, not just better prompts
items.streamSummary: A new preprint introduces Total Simulated Survey Error, an end-to-end framework for identifying validity threats when LLMs are used as synthetic survey respondents. It treats error as something that can enter throughout the simulation lifecycle, not only through a bad prompt. The framework is especially useful for documenting population assumptions, design choices, measurement problems, model biases, and generalization limits. It is a methods proposal with an illustrative case study, not evidence that the framework itself eliminates those errors.

items.streamTitle: Air Force AI experiments are measuring the human decision process, not just software performance
items.streamSummary: The Department of the Air Force’s latest DASH experiment put battle managers, a Space Force operator, researchers, and software developers together to test modular AI tools that generate target-action recommendations and courses of action. AFRL and the 711th Human Performance Wing also measured operator workload and process performance. The Air Force reports faster decision processes and freed cognitive resources, while emphasizing a government-owned plug-and-play architecture for comparing vendor tools. The public account does not provide detailed effect sizes or error rates, so operational effectiveness cannot yet be independently judged.
items.attribution: 505th Command and Control Wing / U.S. Air Force

items.streamTitle: U.S. agencies warn that frontier AI capabilities are being copied through industrial-scale distillation
items.streamSummary: NSA, FBI, and CISA released a joint advisory alleging that China-based AI companies are conducting large-scale distillation campaigns against U.S. frontier models to extract restricted or proprietary capabilities for their own training. The agencies say the activity is distributed across multiple providers and infrastructure services to avoid detection, and they published TTPs and mitigations for defenders. Distillation itself is a legitimate machine-learning technique; the national-security claim concerns allegedly abusive use at scale. The advisory reflects a U.S. government assessment rather than independent proof of every alleged campaign.

items.streamTitle: Cognitive training may transfer in one direction but not the reverse
items.streamSummary: A meta-analysis of 55 working-memory training studies found a small but reliable asymmetry: training that required active updating transferred to simpler span tasks, while span training did not reliably transfer back to updating. The pattern also appeared in some outcomes beyond working memory. This challenges the idea that transfer depends only on how similar two tasks are. The effects are modest, and the meta-analysis cannot determine which proposed mechanism—greater cognitive demand, broader resource recruitment, or another factor—causes the asymmetry.
items.attribution: Fu et al. — Psychonomic Bulletin & Review

items.streamTitle: AI advice increased acceptance of bad recommendations, but time pressure did not make it worse
items.streamSummary: Military cadets and officers in a simulated drone-strike task were more likely to follow wrong or morally questionable recommendations when AI assistance was present. Unexpectedly, high time pressure did not further increase AI reliance or significantly change the moral decisions by itself. Participants also reported less responsibility when using AI, especially under pressure, while seeming to reclaim responsibility when the system was clearly wrong. The study is a controlled simulation rather than an operational test, so it should not be read as a measured battlefield effect.

items.streamTitle: A civilian public-safety program was linked to sizable drops in reported crime at San Francisco intersections
items.streamSummary: A quasi-experimental evaluation of San Francisco’s Urban Alchemy program compared 41 intersections with civilian safety practitioners against 583 untreated intersections over five years. Deployment was associated with about a 20% reduction in total reported crime and a 26.7% reduction in behavioral-health-related incidents, while property crime did not change and some other offense results depended on the model. The design is stronger than a simple before-and-after comparison, but the outcome is recorded police incidents, which can change because of reporting or police-contact patterns as well as underlying behavior.

items.streamTitle: Many LLM agents miss their assigned values before the simulation even begins
items.streamSummary: A World Values Survey–grounded simulation tested 1,200 LLM personas across roughly 4,000 conversations. More than half failed to express the value profiles they had been assigned at the outset, while only 2–7% showed later value drift. Removing demographic details helped some models but did not fix the broader mismatch. The result shifts a key validation question upstream: before studying how synthetic societies change over time, researchers need to verify that the agents actually represent their intended starting states. The study is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed.

items.streamTitle: Why people think they were excluded changes the emotional response
items.streamSummary: Four preregistered studies with 1,757 participants found that exclusion framed as a consequence of one’s own norm violation produced more guilt, shame, and self-directed anger than exclusion without that explanation. Perceived deservingness tracked these reactions most consistently, while gender-based exclusion did not produce the same self-directed pattern. The work shows that exclusion is not one uniform psychological experience. The proposed mechanism is plausible but not fully identified because key mediation measures were collected at the same time as the outcomes.
items.attribution: Damp & Rudert — Journal of Experimental Social Psychology

items.streamTitle: Threatening social comparison hurt performance without making people quit
items.streamSummary: A randomized study of 129 students found that threatening peer-comparison feedback increased negative affect, reduced commitment, and worsened working-memory performance. Yet participants were no less likely to volunteer to repeat the task. The result suggests social comparison can change emotion, coping, and performance without changing immediate persistence. The study was not preregistered and used a university sample, so broader behavioral effects need replication.

items.streamTitle: Romania says it stopped a Russian-directed sabotage reconnaissance operation
items.streamSummary: Romania’s SRI says it stopped a Russian-coordinated sabotage operation involving a Russian citizen allegedly tasked to photograph military sites, critical infrastructure, and Ukrainian cargo aircraft. SRI says the pattern resembles other Russian-linked networks using low-friction support tasks. The case strengthens concern about recruitment funnels, but the underlying intelligence is not fully public, so outside observers cannot independently verify the attribution.

items.streamTitle: A new personalization method learns when it has enough user data
items.streamSummary: A new arXiv paper proposes ENOUGH, a personalization method that adds user-history records one at a time and learns when to stop. Across six tasks, the authors report stronger personalization utility with less context than retrieval-based baselines. The idea matters for persona systems because irrelevant biography can add cost or distortion. It remains a preprint, and task performance does not establish psychological fidelity to real users.
